fca-disp-1-6-2r.title: FCA Handbook DISP 1.6.2R, complaints time limit rules
fca-disp-1-6-2r.cite: A firm must send a final response, or a written response explaining why it cannot yet do so, by the end of eight weeks after receiving the complaint.

fca-disp-1.title: FCA Handbook DISP 1, Treating complainants fairly
fca-disp-1.cite: Prescribes acknowledgement, investigation, final response content and referral rights for FCA-authorised firms handling eligible complainants.

ofcom-gc-c4.title: Ofcom General Condition C4 and its annexed approved complaints code of practice
ofcom-gc-c4.cite: Providers must have and comply with complaints procedures meeting the minimum standards set out in the Ofcom approved complaints code of practice for customer service and complaints handling, and must be a member of an approved ADR scheme (C4.3).

ofcom-adr-six-weeks.title: Ofcom statement, review of ADR in the telecoms sector, 8 July 2025

si-2009-309.cite: The responsible body must acknowledge the complaint not later than 3 working days after the day on which it receives it. The relevant period for response is 6 months from receipt unless a longer period is agreed.

ofgem-slc-0.title: Ofgem electricity and gas supply standard licence conditions, SLC 0, Standards of Conduct
ofgem-slc-0.cite: Suppliers must treat domestic customers fairly, including those in vulnerable situations, and satisfy themselves that their actions result in vulnerable consumers being treated fairly.

ofgem-slc-26.title: Ofgem supply standard licence conditions, SLC 26, Priority Services Register
ofgem-slc-26.cite: Duty on the supplier to establish a Priority Services Register, share information and offer additional support to customers on it, taking all reasonable steps to identify customers in vulnerable situations.

uk261.title: Assimilated Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, UK261
uk261.cite: Establishes compensation and assistance rights on denied boarding, cancellation and long delay, including duties of care during disruption.

caa-adr.title: UK Civil Aviation Authority, making a claim
caa-adr.cite: A passenger dissatisfied with the airline's final response, or waiting more than eight weeks for one, may escalate to an approved ADR provider or to the CAA's Passenger Advice and Complaints Team.

eu-ai-act-art-50.title: EU AI Act Article 50, transparency obligations

eu-ai-act-omnibus.title: EU AI Act Omnibus, political agreement 7 May 2026, in force 27 July 2026
eu-ai-act-omnibus.cite: Annex III high-risk use cases extended to 2 December 2027 and Annex I embedded high-risk systems to 2 August 2028.

retail-baseline.title: No sector-specific statutory complaint-handling regime identified for general retail
retail-baseline.cite: General consumer law applies. No regulator-mandated complaint timetable, approved code or ADR membership duty of the kind Ofcom, the FCA, Ofgem and the CAA impose was found for general retail.

education-an-appeal-of-a-letter-of-decis.title: Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA) Complaints Policy
education-an-appeal-of-a-letter-of-decis.cite: An appeal of a Letter of Decision regarding an equitable services complaint governed by ESEA Section 8503 shall be filed with ED within thirty (30) calendar days after notice of the Letter of Decision.

education-all-maintained-schools-and-mai.title: Education Act 2002
education-all-maintained-schools-and-mai.cite: All maintained schools and maintained nursery schools must have and published procedures to deal with all complaints relating to their school and any community facilities or services that the school provides for which there are no separate statutory procedure.

education-it-is-an-offence-for-a-governm.title: State Records Act 2000 (WA)

education-schools-must-take-reasonable-s.title: U.S. Code
education-schools-must-take-reasonable-s.cite: Schools must take reasonable steps to have service providers capable of maintaining appropriate safeguards for customer information.

education-schools-must-establish-a-lawfu.title: Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018)
education-schools-must-establish-a-lawfu.cite: Schools must establish a lawful basis for processing children's data and must have explicit consent or a clear legal basis for processing special category data such as health information.

education-educational-institutions-must-.title: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)

pharma_life_sciences-pharma-companies-mu.cite: Pharma companies must have documented SOPs for handling complaints, timely complaint review, investigation requirements if a complaint indicates possible failure of the drug to meet specifications, batch record examination for every quality-related complaint, and complaint records must be maintained for at least 1 year after the product's expiration date.

pharma_life_sciences-a-designated-person.title: EU GMP (European Good Manufacturing Practices) Guidelines Chapter 8

public_sector-special-category-data-may-.title: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018

public_sector-firms-must-ensure-that-cus.title: FCA Consumer Duty

technology_software-manufacturers-must-e.cite: Manufacturers must establish and maintain complaint handling procedures that cover receipt, review, and evaluation of complaints, including investigation, regulatory reporting, and effective post-market vigilance, and linkage to corrective action and preventive actions (CAPA).

technology_software-organisations-must-a.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA)
technology_software-organisations-must-a.cite: Organisations must acknowledge complaints within 30 days of receipt and investigate without undue delay, with mandatory information requirements and timeframes for handling data protection complaints made directly to the data controller.

technology_software-special-category-per.title: UK GDPR - Article 9
technology_software-special-category-per.cite: Special category personal data (including health data, biometric data, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, genetic data, trade union membership, sex life, and sexual orientation) requires explicit consent and additional safeguards to protect individuals' rights and freedoms.

financial_services.label: Financial services
financial_services.regime: FCA DISP plus Consumer Duty. A complaint carries a statutory clock, a prescribed final response and a right of referral to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

CAP-10.why: DISP prescribes acknowledgement, timetable and the referral wording a final response must carry. Deviation is a rule breach with external consequence, which is the band 90 anchor.

CAP-15.why: Complaint files are subject to FCA supervision and firms report complaints data, so the work carries a formal audit trail open to regulator inspection.

CAP-11.why: A missed eight-week deadline is itself a breach, so an undetected error draws regulatory attention rather than only requiring correction.

CAP-08.why: Where an advisor drafts the final response it is a binding external document. Firms vary in whether the front line drafts it, so this is scored from job descriptions rather than from the rules.

CAP-03.why: Requires knowing why the rules exist and where exceptions apply, not only recognising standard cases: eligibility, jurisdiction and time bars are all judgement calls under DISP.

CAP-11.why: An FOS determination is binding on the firm, so a mishandled complaint creates legal liability rather than reputational damage alone. Scored from the ombudsman's binding power rather than from a rule that states the consequence.

CAP-15.why: Contact centre quality assurance forms part of the evidence a firm shows the FCA on complaint handling, so the work is inspected rather than internally signed off.

CAP-10.why: The procedures the manager enforces are themselves prescribed by DISP.

CAP-15.why: Complaints reporting is submitted to the regulator and attested, so assurance work is externally assured rather than internally audited. Scored from the reporting duty rather than from a rule naming the analyst.
Consumer Duty places individual accountability on a named senior manager, which is the band 90 anchor. Scored from the Duty's accountability structure rather than from a rule naming this job title.

telecom_media.label: Telecoms and media
telecom_media.regime: Ofcom General Condition C4 and its annexed approved complaints code, with compulsory ADR membership. The escalation window fell from eight weeks to six on 8 April 2026.
telecom_media.scopeNote: The evidence is telecoms-specific. General Condition C4 binds communications providers serving residential, small business and not-for-profit customers. A media business in this sector that is not a communications provider is not covered by it, and this lens overstates its position.

CAP-10.why: The approved code is a minimum standard annexed to a general condition, so departure from it is a breach of the provider's authorisation.

CAP-15.why: Ofcom has run enforcement programmes into complaints handling, so the work is subject to regulator inspection.

CAP-13.why: No change to the band, recorded because the escalation window shortened from eight weeks to six on 8 April 2026 and any timetable built on the old figure is now wrong.

CAP-10.why: No change to the band. Recorded because the six-week ADR trigger replaced the eight-week one on 8 April 2026 and the deadline the role works to has moved.

CAP-03.why: The code sets out when ADR letters are due and to whom the rules apply, which turns on customer classification: residential, small business and not-for-profit are in scope and others are not.

CAP-15.why: Compliance with the annexed code is inspected by Ofcom rather than signed off internally.

healthcare.label: Healthcare
healthcare.regime: SI 2009/309 sets a statutory complaints procedure for NHS bodies and local authority social care, with a three working day acknowledgement and a six month relevant period.

CAP-14.why: Health records are special-category data and their exposure causes serious harm, which is the band 90 anchor rather than the band 70 one the base profile carries.

CAP-10.why: The acknowledgement deadline is set by statutory instrument, so missing it is a breach of regulation and not an internal service failure.

CAP-15.why: Complaint handling is inspected by the Care Quality Commission and reviewable by the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman.

CAP-13.why: Three working days to acknowledge is a same-week statutory obligation rather than the same-day norm the base profile assumes, and the clock starts on receipt anywhere in the body.

CAP-03.why: The regulations require the body to offer to agree the handling and response period at acknowledgement, which is a judgement about scope made against the statute.

CAP-14.why: Oversight of a contact centre handling patient records reaches the same special-category data as the front line.
Quality sampling reads the case files themselves, so the analyst holds the same records.

CAP-15.why: The regulations place the duty on the responsible body and require an annual report, which is external assurance. Scored from the body-level duty rather than from a rule naming this job title.

energy_utilities.label: Energy and utilities
energy_utilities.regime: Ofgem standard licence conditions. SLC 0 requires fair treatment of customers in vulnerable situations and SLC 26 establishes the Priority Services Register.

CAP-10.why: Identifying a customer in a vulnerable situation and registering them is a licence obligation, so failing to act on the signs is a breach of the supply licence.

CAP-15.why: Ofgem has opened investigations into supplier compliance with SLC 0 and SLC 26, so day to day conduct is subject to regulator inspection.

CAP-11.why: A missed vulnerability signal reaches a customer who may be at risk and draws regulatory attention, which is the band 70 anchor.

CAP-14.why: Priority Services Register entries record health conditions and disability, which is special-category data held under a licence duty. Scored from what the register contains rather than from a data protection rule naming it.

CAP-15.why: Ofgem has issued guidance on its expectations for consumers to be able to contact their supplier, making contact centre performance a licence matter open to inspection.

SLC 0 requires the supplier to satisfy itself that its actions result in fair treatment, which is a standing attestation rather than a periodic audit. Scored from the licence wording rather than from a rule naming this job title.

transport_logistics.label: Transport and logistics
transport_logistics.regime: UK261 sets compensation and duty of care on delay, cancellation and denied boarding. The CAA takes escalation after eight weeks or an unsatisfactory final response.
transport_logistics.scopeNote: The evidence is passenger aviation only. UK261 confers rights on air passengers and says nothing about freight, shipping or road logistics, which sit in this sector and have no equivalent regime. For a business that does not carry passengers by air this lens overstates its position and should be read as not yet researched.

CAP-02.why: Entitlement depends on a chain: distance band, delay at destination, notice given, and whether the cause was within the airline's control. An early error changes the answer, which is the band 50 anchor.

CAP-10.why: Duty of care during disruption is a regulatory entitlement, not a service gesture, and withholding it is a breach.

CAP-15.why: The CAA runs a UK261 compliance programme into air passenger rights, so handling is subject to regulator inspection.

CAP-02.why: The extraordinary circumstances defence, re-routing obligations and compensation bands interact, so the reasoning branches rather than running to a single conclusion.

CAP-03.why: Knowing when the extraordinary circumstances defence holds is expert knowledge of why the rule exists, not recognition of a standard case.

CAP-13.why: Duty of care during live disruption is owed while passengers are waiting at the airport, so delay in standing up the response causes the harm the rule addresses. Scored from the nature of the duty rather than from a stated response time.

retail_consumer.label: Retail and consumer
retail_consumer.regime: General consumer law only. No sector regulator imposes a complaint timetable, an approved code or compulsory ADR membership, which is why this vertical is the baseline the others are read against.

education.label: Education
education.regime: Education sector complaint procedures and data protection regulations

CAP-03.why: Operating simultaneously under ESEA complaint procedures, GDPR/DPA 2018 special-category data rules, GLBA/FTC safeguarding requirements and state records law requires expert-level recognition of exceptions and the reasons behind each regime's rules, matching the 70 band rather than routine practitioner knowledge.

CAP-10.why: ESEA Section 8503 imposes a strict 30-calendar-day appeal deadline and the Education Act 2002 mandates published complaint procedures, so deviation from prescribed steps becomes a reportable event rather than a justifiable exception.

CAP-11.why: Under DPA 2018/GDPR, mishandling special-category student data (health, disability, psychological-pedagogical) exposes the school to regulatory attention and reputational harm, moving error cost beyond internal correction to the 70 band.

CAP-15.why: The WA State Records Act 2000 makes unauthorised removal, destruction or transfer of government records a personal offence carrying a $10,000 penalty, creating individual legal accountability that matches the 90 band rather than mere audit-trail review.

The State Records Act 2000 (WA) makes unauthorised removal, destruction or transfer of government records a criminal offence for the individual employee, with a $10,000 penalty; this matches the CAP-15 band-90 anchor of 'individual accountability with legal or licensing consequence' rather than the base role's informal-review level. GDPR Article 30's requirement for a Record of Processing Activities further formalises the audit trail the role must maintain.

CAP-11.why: GLBA (15 USC 6801(b)/6805(b)(2)) and FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR 313.3(n), 314.1-5) require schools to keep customer/student information under contractual safeguards; an advisor's mishandling of that data is not merely reworked internally but exposes the institution to regulatory attention, moving the role past CAP-11's 'reaches colleagues or customers' band into 'regulatory attention or reputational damage'.

CAP-10.why: ESEA Section 8503 imposes a strict 30-calendar-day statutory appeal window for complaint decisions, and the Education Act 2002 Part 7 requires published, mandated complaint procedures; a CSM handling education complaints must follow these to the letter, matching the 'strict compliance; deviation is a reportable event' anchor rather than the base 'defined procedures... deviation must be justified'.

CAP-14.why: GDPR Article 9 requires an additional lawful basis for processing special-category data such as health, disability or psychological-pedagogical information about students, which a CSM routinely encounters when resolving service issues; this matches the 'special-category personal data... regulated health records' anchor rather than the base 'confidential commercial or limited personal data' level.

CAP-15.why: GDPR Article 30 mandates a Record of Processing Activities across the student lifecycle, and the WA State Records Act 2000 makes unauthorised removal or destruction of government records a criminal offence with financial penalties; this creates a formal audit trail subject to regulatory inspection, well above the base 'no review' level.

CAP-08.why: ESEA Section 8503 requires issuance of a formal 'Letter of Decision' that is appealable to a federal agency within 30 days; this is a binding document for an external audience, matching band 70 rather than routine internal correspondence.

CAP-10.why: ESEA Section 8503 sets a strict 30-calendar-day statutory appeal deadline for equitable-services complaints; missing it forecloses a legal right and constitutes a breach with external consequence, matching band 90 rather than band 70's 'reportable event' standard.

CAP-11.why: State Records Act 2000 (WA) makes unauthorised destruction, removal or transfer of government records an offence carrying a $10,000 penalty, so record-handling errors in complaint files trigger regulatory/legal consequence, matching band 70.

CAP-15.why: Complaint decisions are subject to a formal external appeal to a federal education agency under ESEA Section 8503, and Education Act 2002 Part 7 mandates published, auditable complaint procedures, indicating a formal audit trail subject to regulator scrutiny (band 70) rather than informal internal sign-off.

CAP-03.why: Handling education complaints correctly requires practitioner-level familiarity with multiple overlapping statutory regimes (ESEA Section 8503 equitable-services appeals, Education Act 2002 complaint procedures, GDPR Article 9 special-category data rules), moving beyond generic terminology to recognising standard regulated cases, matching the 50-band anchor.

CAP-08.why: ESEA Section 8503 requires issuance of a formal Letter of Decision that can be appealed to ED within 30 days; this is a binding document for an external regulatory audience, matching the 70-band anchor rather than routine internal documents.

CAP-10.why: ESEA Section 8503 imposes a strict 30-calendar-day statutory appeal window; missing it forecloses the complainant's appeal rights, an external legal consequence matching the 90-band anchor ('deviation is a breach with external consequence') rather than merely a reportable internal event.

CAP-11.why: Under GLBA Sections 501/505(b)(2) and FTC 16 CFR 314.1-5, failures in safeguarding customer/student data during complaint or service handling can trigger regulatory attention, matching the 70-band anchor ('errors cause financial loss, regulatory attention, or reputational damage') rather than mere internal rework.

CAP-15.why: The State Records Act 2000 (WA) makes unauthorised destruction or removal of government records a personal offence carrying a $10,000 penalty, creating individual legal accountability that matches the 90-band anchor ('externally assured; individual accountability with legal or licensing consequence') rather than a standard internal audit trail.

insurance.label: Insurance
insurance.regime: Insurance regulatory compliance including claims handling, complaints procedures, record retention, and vulnerable customer protections across multiple jurisdictions

CAP-03.why: FCA Consumer Duty (PRIN 2A.2.22R) and GDPR Art.9(2)/DPA 2018 Sch.1 Para 20 require recognising when special-category or vulnerable-customer exceptions apply and why they exist, matching the 'expert knowledge; recognises exceptions' band rather than routine practitioner knowledge.

CAP-08.why: Quebec's complaint regulation (ss.5-10, 30) and Texas 28 TAC 13.492 mandate specific, regulator-defined written acknowledgments and consumer-facing complaint summaries with prescribed content, i.e. binding external documents rather than routine internal correspondence.

CAP-15.why: The Quebec complaint-handling regulation (effective July 1, 2025) newly mandates formal complaint policies and audit-ready records subject to regulator review, reaffirming rather than shifting the existing 'formal audit trail; regulator inspection' band.

CAP-03.why: FCA Consumer Duty vulnerable-customer monitoring and multi-jurisdiction complaint regimes require practitioner-level knowledge of specific regulatory categories and standard cases (vulnerability triggers, complaint classification), matching band 50 rather than generic field familiarity.

CAP-08.why: Quebec's complaint regulation (in force July 1, 2025) mandates acknowledgment letters and summaries with specified, regulator-defined content for external consumers, requiring structured documents beyond routine correspondence.

CAP-11.why: Undetected errors in complaint handling or vulnerable-customer monitoring under FCA Consumer Duty and cross-jurisdiction complaint rules can trigger regulatory attention or reportable failures, not just internal rework, matching band 70.

Errors in complaint handling or record management in insurance trigger regulatory attention under regimes like the Quebec complaint regulation and CIMA's Internal Controls Rule, moving beyond internal rework to band 70 ('regulatory attention or reputational damage').

CAP-14.why: GDPR Article 9 classifies health data processed for insurance purposes as special-category data requiring specific safeguards (DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Para 20), matching band 70 ('special-category personal data, regulated financial or health records') rather than generic confidential data.

CAP-03.why: FCA Consumer Duty (PRIN 2A.2.22R) requires ongoing reactive and proactive identification of vulnerable customers and maintenance of an evidence trail, which demands expert-level recognition of exceptions and the reasons behind protection rules rather than routine practitioner knowledge.

CAP-08.why: Quebec's Regulation respecting complaint processing (ss.5-10, 30) and 28 Tex. Admin. Code §13.492 mandate specific, regulator-prescribed wording and content in complaint acknowledgments and consumer-facing policy summaries, so the exact language used carries direct regulatory consequence.

CAP-10.why: Quebec's Regulation respecting complaint processing and dispute resolution (in force July 1, 2025) and 28 Tex. Admin. Code §13.492 impose strict, dated procedural steps (e.g. 7-day acknowledgment) whose breach is externally reportable; band stays at the ceiling but the underlying rule is newly in force, so the change is flagged for visibility.

CAP-03.why: Insurance regulatory regimes (FCA Consumer Duty vulnerable-customer rules, multi-jurisdictional complaint/retention regimes) require the manager to recognise standard regulated cases (vulnerable customer status, complaint categorisation, retention triggers) rather than apply general knowledge, matching band 50 practitioner-level recognition rather than the generic band 30 familiarity.
